scenario: AITA For Selling My Former Roommates Games | So a few years ago I was renting this place with this dude and we were on a lease. When the lease was nearing it's end he just peaced out. We're talking took most of everything leaving only the last bit of his half of rent and a few things he said in a note he didn't want to bring with him. Thing with where I live is that if you don't discard of things on your own when you move out the landlord can pay to have someone remove the stuff. We're talking cases of dudes having $250 taken off their deposit just for some dude to take 3 milk crates of things to the dump. It's a rip off. I texted and emailed him for 2 weeks asking to pick these things up or take them to the dump but he never responded. So I took most of his things to the dump but he also had around 60 video games for PS4. So I figured I'd sell them. There is a local game store where they buy used games and they gave me $600 for all of his games. Well cut to last week and I was at a party he was at and we were polite. He then asks how the move out was and I said good, and naturally he asked what I did with his stuff. He got mad when he found out I sold his games but I told him that I tried to get him to grab these things but he never reached out. He's now calling me an asshole and asking me to pay him back. I checked and legally there's nothing there but now I'm wondering if I'm the asshole for doing this.

Okay, let's tackle this scenario. The user is asking if they're the asshole (AITA) for selling their former roommate's video games. The roommate left without taking his stuff, and after multiple attempts to get him to pick it up or dispose of it, the user sold the games for $600. Now the roommate is upset and wants his money back.

First, I need to consider the moral aspects here. The roommate didn't take his belongings, which is his responsibility. The user tried to communicate for two weeks but got no response. Legally, in many places, if someone leaves belongings behind, the landlord or the remaining tenant might have the right to dispose of them after a certain period. The user's action of selling the games might be within their rights, especially since the roommate didn't claim them.

However, morally, even if it's legal, is it right to sell someone else's property without their consent? The roommate might feel that his games were his personal items, and selling them without permission is a violation of trust. The user's intention was to get rid of the items to avoid the landlord's fees, which is a practical reason. But the roommate's reaction is strong, indicating he values his games and feels wronged.

The key points are: the roommate abandoned his stuff, the user tried to resolve it, and the sale was a last resort. The roommate's anger might stem from not being informed or not having a chance to retrieve his items. The user didn't take the games for personal gain but sold them to cover costs. However, the roommate's expectation might be that he should get his things back, not that they're sold.

In some ethical frameworks, taking someone's property without consent is wrong, even if they left it. But others might argue that after a reasonable attempt to retrieve, selling is acceptable. The user's actions were proactive in trying to handle the situation, which could be seen as responsible. However, the lack of communication after the sale might have exacerbated the issue.

Considering all this, the action might be legally acceptable but morally questionable. The roommate's feelings are valid, and the user could have handled it better by informing him before selling. But since the roommate didn't respond to initial requests, the user's action might be justified. However, the moral acceptability depends on whether the user should have kept the items or informed the roommate. Since the roommate didn't act, the user's sale might be acceptable, but the moral judgment could lean towards 0 because of the lack of communication and taking someone's property without consent.
